clinicalPearls: Defined by acute severe liver injury with coagulopathy (INR generally above 1.5) and any degree of encephalopathy in a patient without pre-existing chronic liver disease, developing within about 26 weeks of illness onset

Speed of onset matters clinically: hyperacute presentations (encephalopathy within roughly a week or two of jaundice) are typically from acetaminophen toxicity or viral hepatitis and, despite dramatic cerebral edema risk, often carry better spontaneous recovery odds than slower subacute forms
Acetaminophen overdose and drug-induced liver injury are the leading causes in resource-rich settings, while viral hepatitis (especially hepatitis B and E) dominates in many other regions
Cerebral edema and raised intracranial pressure are the most feared early complications and a major cause of death, particularly in hyperacute presentations
Coagulopathy in ALF reflects a rebalanced but fragile hemostatic state rather than pure bleeding tendency; INR is used mainly for prognosis and monitoring, not as a routine transfusion trigger
Early transfer to a liver transplant center should be considered as soon as ALF is recognized, since deterioration can be rapid and unpredictable
Look actively for a treatable cause (acetaminophen, autoimmune hepatitis, Wilson disease, HELLP/acute fatty liver of pregnancy, vascular causes) since specific therapy can be life-saving
Infection and sepsis are common complications during the course of ALF and should be surveilled for proactively rather than only when clinically obvious
harrison.pathophysiology: Massive hepatocyte necrosis or dysfunction outstrips the liver's regenerative capacity, causing simultaneous failure of synthetic function (coagulation factors, albumin), detoxification (ammonia, other neurotoxins), and metabolic homeostasis. Accumulating ammonia and inflammatory mediators drive astrocyte swelling and cerebral edema, producing hepatic encephalopathy and raised intracranial pressure. The systemic inflammatory response and impaired hepatic clearance of pathogens also predispose to circulatory dysfunction, renal impairment, and secondary infection, contributing to a multiorgan failure picture.
additionalDifferentials: Decompensated chronic liver disease (cirrhosis with acute-on-chronic liver failure)
Severe acute hepatitis without encephalopathy (acute liver injury short of failure)
Acute Budd-Chiari syndrome and other vascular liver outflow obstruction
Acute fatty liver of pregnancy / HELLP syndrome
Malignant infiltration of the liver causing acute hepatic dysfunction
infectionMimics: Viral hepatitis A, B, D (with B), and E
Severe sepsis with secondary hepatic dysfunction
nonInfectiousMimics: Idiosyncratic drug-induced liver injury (including certain antituberculous and antiepileptic agents, and herbal/dietary supplements)
Wilson disease presenting with acute decompensation
Acute fatty liver of pregnancy and HELLP syndrome
additionalInvestigations: Prothrombin time/INR — core diagnostic criterion and key prognostic marker
Arterial ammonia level — correlates with risk of cerebral edema and severe encephalopathy
Acetaminophen level and detailed drug/toxin/supplement history — identifies the most common treatable etiology
Viral hepatitis serologies (A, B, C, D, E) and, where relevant, HSV/CMV testing — identifies infectious causes
Autoimmune markers (ANA, smooth muscle antibody, immunoglobulins) and ceruloplasmin/copper studies — screens for autoimmune hepatitis and Wilson disease
Doppler ultrasound of hepatic and portal vasculature — evaluates for vascular outflow obstruction
Arterial blood gas, lactate, and renal function — assess systemic perfusion and evolving multiorgan dysfunction
Blood and other cultures with a low threshold for infection screening — ALF patients are prone to occult sepsis
redFlags: Any new alteration in mental status or asterixis in a patient with acute severe liver injury — signals encephalopathy and true liver failure
Rapidly rising INR with jaundice — suggests impending or established failure requiring urgent transplant center contact
Signs of raised intracranial pressure (hypertension with bradycardia, pupillary changes, posturing) — medical emergency
Hemodynamic instability, oliguria, or lactic acidosis — herald multiorgan involvement
Grade III–IV encephalopathy — generally warrants intensive care and consideration of airway protection
Any suspicion of acetaminophen ingestion, even with a vague or denied history — treatable and time-sensitive
pitfalls: Assuming a normal or mildly elevated bilirubin excludes liver failure — hyperacute acetaminophen-related ALF can present with striking coagulopathy and encephalopathy before marked jaundice develops

Using INR alone to guide prophylactic correction with plasma products — this does not reflect true bleeding risk in the rebalanced coagulopathy of ALF and can complicate assessment of hepatic synthetic recovery
Delaying transfer to a transplant-capable center while pursuing additional outpatient-type workup — deterioration can be abrupt
Overlooking a treatable etiology (Wilson disease, autoimmune hepatitis, pregnancy-related liver disease) because acetaminophen or viral hepatitis seems statistically likely
harrison.prognosis: Outcome depends heavily on etiology and speed of onset: hyperacute presentations from acetaminophen or hepatitis A/E often have a better chance of spontaneous recovery than subacute presentations, which have lower native-liver survival. Emergency liver transplantation substantially improves survival in appropriately selected patients who do not recover spontaneously.
references: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 22e — Chapter on Acute Liver Failure
management: Aetiology-specific therapy: N-acetylcysteine for paracetamol toxicity, nucleos(t)ide analogues for hepatitis B, aciclovir for herpes simplex, and immunosuppression, chelation or delivery for autoimmune, Wilson and pregnancy-related causes respectively.
Early discussion with and transfer to a liver transplant centre, with emergency transplantation assessment against recognised prognostic criteria.
Neuroprotection against cerebral oedema and raised intracranial pressure through head-up positioning, avoidance of hyponatraemia, sedation and hyperosmolar therapy with mannitol or hypertonic saline.
Intensive-care organ support with vasopressors for circulatory failure, renal replacement therapy for acute kidney injury and ammonia clearance, and correction of hypoglycaemia.
Judicious management of coagulopathy, reserving clotting-factor and platelet replacement for active bleeding or procedures rather than correcting the deranged INR alone.
Active surveillance for infection with a low threshold for broad-spectrum antimicrobial and antifungal therapy.
Close monitoring of INR, arterial ammonia, glucose, lactate and neurological status, with multidisciplinary hepatology, intensive-care and transplant-surgery input.
